We construct a fractured structure, in the sense of Lurie, on the $\infty$-topos of condensed anima. This fractured structure allows us to better comprehend various properties of condensed anima - we use it to exhibit an explicit collection of jointly conservative points for condensed anima. To rule out further candidates for fractured structures, we analyze limits in the category of extremally disconnected spaces. In particular, we show that it does not admit all fibers, answering a question from Clausen.

1. Introduction 1.1. From petit vs. gros to fractured topoi Topos theory was introduced as a categorical method to study topologies in a variety of settings. However, somewhat surprisingly, it permitted two parallel approaches. On the one hand, there are topoi which capture the data of one particular space, such as the topos of sheaves on a topological space or the étale topos of a scheme. On the other hand, there are topoi which include many spaces at once, such as sheaves on the site of all topological spaces or sheaves on the site of all schemes. Motivated by their French origin, these two classes of topoi are often informally referred to as petit and gros topoi, respectively. As a result, right from the start a central theme in topos theory has been to bridge these two parallel approaches. For example, already in [ 5 , Exposé VII, Proposition 4.1] the authors observe that étale sheaves on a scheme X X sit fully faithfully inside the big étale topos sliced over X X , resulting in the following crucial observation [ 5 , Exposé VII, under Proposition 4.1] : Pour l’étude de la cohomologie des faisceaux, il est essentiellement équivalent de travailler avec le petit site étale X e ´ ​ t X_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}} , ou le gros site étale ( Sch / X ) e ´ ​ t (\mathrm{Sch}/X)_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}} . They establish a similar relationship between the petit and gros topos of a topological space [ 4 , Exposé IV, 4.10.4] . Other examples of this phenomenon include the Zariski site [ 45 , Tag 020Z ] , the crystalline site [ 45 , Tag 07IJ ] , and the pro-étale site [ 45 , Tag 098Q ] , among others. It is hence unsurprising that various efforts have been made to axiomatize the relation between petit and gros topoi. One successful method is the theory of fractured ∞ \infty -topoi due to Lurie [ 34 ] , motivated by Carchedi [ 10 ] . 1 1 1 Another related approach is given by cohesive ∞ \infty -topoi , which will not be our focus here. See 2.5 for a discussion of the relationship between these two approaches. A fractured structure on an ∞ \infty -topos 𝒳 \mathscr{X} is a (not necessarily full) subcategory 𝒳 corp \mathscr{X}^{\mathrm{corp}} , such that the inclusion functor admits a right adjoint satisfying various axioms. See 2.1 for a detailed definition. The conditions in particular imply that for an object X X in 𝒳 corp \mathscr{X}^{\mathrm{corp}} , the slice category 𝒳 / X corp \mathscr{X}^{\mathrm{corp}}_{/X} sits fully faithfully inside 𝒳 / X \mathscr{X}_{/X} ( 2.3 ). Thus, thinking intuitively of 𝒳 \mathscr{X} as a gros topos and 𝒳 corp \mathscr{X}^{\mathrm{corp}} as a petit topos, the fractured structure axiomatically realizes the anticipated relationship between gros and petit topoi in a very general setting. As one might expect, many situations where gros and petit topoi occur are in fact examples of fractured ∞ \infty -topoi. This includes some of the aforementioned examples, such as the classical Zariski site and étale site [ 34 , Examples 20.6.4.1 and 20.6.4.2] , but also their analogues from spectral algebraic geometry [ 34 , Examples 20.6.4.4 and 20.6.4.5] . Beyond algebraic geometry, further examples of fractured structures have been exhibited in differential geometry [ 15 , 16 ] , global equivariant homotopy theory [ 18 ] , and the theory of six functor formalisms [ 17 , Section 7.3] . 1.2. Condensed anima as a gros topos The idea of a topological space is ubiquitous in mathematics and plays a prominent role in algebra, for instance via topological abelian groups. These are notoriously ill-behaved, and in particular do not form an abelian category, a crucial requirement to perform homological algebra. This has impeded progress in areas in which topological groups naturally occur, such as analytic geometry. Solving this issue resulted in the theory of condensed mathematics , developed by Clausen and Scholze [ 42 ] , and independently by Barwick and Haine [ 7 ] , leading to successful applications in analytic geometry [ 43 ] . Fundamentally, the success of condensed mathematics is due to the power of topos theory. By isolating a desirable class of topological spaces, in this case extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff spaces, denoted ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc \mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc} , and then passing to sheaves on them, one obtains the ∞ \infty -topos of condensed anima 𝒞 ​ ond ​ ( 𝒜 ​ n ) ≔ 𝒮 ​ hv 𝒜 ​ n ​ ( ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc ) . \mathscr{C}\mathrm{ond}(\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n})\coloneqq\mathscr{S}\mathrm{hv}_{\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n}}(\mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc}). We will give a more detailed review in Section 2.2 . This construction simultaneously includes examples of interest, in particular all compactly generated topological spaces, while gaining many desirable properties inherent to sheaf categories. Historically, such methods can already be seen in the work of Johnstone, who introduced the topological topos with similar aims [ 28 ] . The theory has risen to prominence in the last few years and has found applications in various areas of mathematics, such as in algebra [ 2 , 9 ] , analysis [ 42 ] , geometry [ 43 , 13 , 21 ] , representation theory [ 23 ] , set theory [ 8 ] and topology [ 37 , 14 , 36 ] . Condensed anima include all (compactly-generated) topological spaces [ 42 , Proposition 1.7] . Hence, from the perspective of Section 1.1 , condensed anima exhibit the behavior of a gros topos. It is therefore natural to ask whether there is a subcategory of condensed anima that gives a fractured structure, making our intuition regarding condensed anima as a gros topos into a rigorous statement. 1.3. Fractured structure on condensed anima In this article, we realize this vision and construct a fractured structure on condensed anima. With 𝒞 ​ ond ​ ( 𝒜 ​ n ) = 𝒮 ​ hv ​ ( ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc ) \mathscr{C}\mathrm{ond}(\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n})=\mathscr{S}\mathrm{hv}(\mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc}) , we choose the collection of open embeddings on extremally disconnected spaces as a base for the corresponding petit topos. Let ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc open \mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc}^{\mathrm{open}} denote the wide subcategory of extremally disconnected spaces spanned by the open embeddings, equipped with a Grothendieck topology given by finitely jointly surjective families of open embeddings. Our main theorem is the following. Theorem A ( 3.7 ) . The left Kan extension of the restriction functor 𝒞 ​ ond open ​ ( 𝒜 ​ n ) ≔ 𝒮 ​ hv ​ ( ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc open ) ⟶ 𝒞 ​ ond ​ ( 𝒜 ​ n ) , \mathscr{C}\mathrm{ond}^{\mathrm{open}}(\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n})\coloneqq\mathscr{S}\mathrm{hv}(\mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc}^{\mathrm{open}})\longrightarrow\mathscr{C}\mathrm{ond}(\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n}), induces a fractured ∞ \infty -topos structure. More precisely, we mean that this functor induces an equivalence onto a subcategory of 𝒞 ​ ond ​ ( 𝒜 ​ n ) \mathscr{C}\mathrm{ond}(\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n}) , and the inclusion of this subcategory is a fractured structure. The philosophy of petit and gros topoi is laid out clearly after passing to slice topoi by the following result. See 3.2 for further details. Theorem B ( 3.11 ) . For every S ∈ ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc S\in\mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc} there is an equivalence 𝒞 ​ ond open ​ ( 𝒜 ​ n ) / open ​ S ≃ 𝒮 ​ hv ​ ( S ) \mathscr{C}\mathrm{ond}^{\mathrm{open}}(\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n})_{/\text{\char 136\relax}_{\mathrm{open}}S}\simeq\mathscr{S}\mathrm{hv}(S) of ∞ \infty -categories. The fractured structure along with the above computation allows us to draw a number of formal consequences and better understand condensed anima. For example, following Clough [ 15 ] , the framework gives us a new constructive proof for the fact that 𝒞 ​ ond ​ ( 𝒜 ​ n ) \mathscr{C}\mathrm{ond}(\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n}) has enough points, and even an explicit collection of such points. Theorem C ( 3.14 ) . The collection of points { 𝒞 ond ( 𝒜 n ) ⟶ 𝒜 n , F ↦ colim U ⊆ S ​ clopen s ∈ U F ( U ) } S ∈ ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc , s ∈ S \left\{\mathscr{C}\mathrm{ond}(\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n})\longrightarrow\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n},\ F\mapsto\operatorname*{colim}_{\begin{subarray}{c}U\subseteq S\ \mathrm{clopen}\\ s\in U\end{subarray}}F(U)\right\}_{S\in\mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc},\ s\in S} is jointly conservative. 1.4. The magical topology of extremally disconnected spaces The choice of open embeddings on extremally disconnected spaces for our petit topos was far from arbitrary. Our last main result aims to show that the construction and study of the fractured structure on 𝒞 ​ ond ​ ( 𝒜 ​ n ) \mathscr{C}\mathrm{ond}(\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n}) relies on very specific point-set topological properties of extremally disconnected spaces. A priori, there are various other constructions one could envision to build fractured structures on condensed anima. One could change the choice of embeddings and even enlarge the base ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc \mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc} to profinite sets or compact Hausdorff spaces, but we show in 4.7 that enlarging the base is not a fruitful approach. Staying within the realm of extremally disconnected spaces, a natural replacement of open embeddings appears to be the collection of all injections. However, we prove in 4.14 that this too does not result in a fractured structure. The main culprit lies in ill-behaved features of the category ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc \mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc} that are imposed by the point-set topological features of extremally disconnected spaces. More precisely, the failure lies in the following conjecture proposed by Clausen ( 4.10 ), which we prove. Theorem D ( 4.13 ) . The category ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc \mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc} does not admit all fibers. Indeed, let β ​ π 1 : β ⁡ ( ℕ × ℕ ) → β ​ ℕ \beta\pi_{1}\colon\beta(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N})\to\beta\mathbb{N} be induced by the projection onto the first coordinate. We show that the fiber over an element p ∈ β ​ ℕ ∖ ℕ p\in\beta\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathbb{N} is not extremally disconnected. Remark 2.12: We warn that the category ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc \mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc} behaves extremely 4 4 4 Pun intended. badly. This has caused us many headaches throughout the project. For example, not even binary products of infinite extremally disconnected spaces exist in ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc \mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc} , see [ 29 , Proposition 2.54] . We will later show that it does not admit all fibers, see 4.13 . Let us moreover remark that every convergent sequence in extremally disconnected spaces is eventually constant [ 20 , Theorem 1.3] . These objects are intimately connected to set theory since every extremally disconnected space is a retract of the Stone–Čech compactification of a discrete space [ 39 , Corollary] . The latter often features in set-theoretic contexts.

Remark 2.13: One primary reason to work with extremally disconnected spaces is that they are precisely the projective objects in 𝒞 ​ ℋ ​ aus \mathscr{C}\mathscr{H}\mathrm{aus} by Gleason [ 20 , Theorem 2.5] , meaning every continuous surjection into an extremally disconnected space admits a section.

Definition 3.1: Let ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc open \mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc}^{\mathrm{open}} be the site consisting of the wide subcategory of ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc \mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc} with maps given by open embeddings and coverings given by finitely jointly surjective families of open embeddings defining a Grothendieck topology τ open \tau_{\mathrm{open}} . We denote by 𝒞 ​ ond open ​ ( 𝒜 ​ n ) ≔ 𝒮 ​ hv ​ ( ℰ ​ xtr ​ 𝒟 ​ isc open ) \mathscr{C}\mathrm{ond}^{\mathrm{open}}(\mathscr{A}\mathrm{n})\coloneqq\mathscr{S}\mathrm{hv}(\mathscr{E}\mathrm{xtr}\mathscr{D}\mathrm{isc}^{\mathrm{open}}) the resulting ∞ \infty -category of sheaves.
